paper_title: DLP Dynamic Layerwise Pruning in Large Language Models
caption: Perplexity of LLaMA1-7B on different validation datasets under varying quantization bits.

model_annotations.Bulgarian: The figure presents three grouped bar charts — (a) WikiText, (b) PTB, and (c) C4 — each illustrating the perplexity of the LLaMA1-7B model under two quantization strategies — “Uniform” (blue bars) and “Ours” (orange bars) — across four levels of quantization bits: 3, 4, 8, and 16. In all three subplots, the horizontal axis represents the number of quantization bits, while the vertical axis measures perplexity on a linear scale, with ranges varying per dataset: approximately 0–30 for WikiText and C4, and 0–400 for PTB. For each quantization bit level, the “Uniform” method consistently yields higher perplexity values than “Ours,” indicating better performance (lower perplexity) for the proposed method across all datasets and bit configurations. In subplot (a) WikiText, perplexity for “Uniform” ranges from ~29 at 3 bits to ~27 at 16 bits, while “Ours” ranges from ~22 to ~18. In subplot (b) PTB, “Uniform” spans from ~400 to ~300, and “Ours” from ~250 to ~185. In subplot (c) C4, “Uniform” decreases from ~28 to ~25, and “Ours” from ~21 to ~18. The bars are grouped by quantization bit level, with no reordering within groups, and the legend is consistently positioned in the top-left corner of each subplot. The visual trend across all datasets shows that as quantization bits increase, perplexity generally decreases for both methods, though the gap between “Uniform” and “Ours” remains consistent or slightly widens at higher bit levels.
model_annotations.English: The figure presents three bar charts—(a) WikiText, (b) PTB, and (c) C4—comparing the perplexity of LLaMA1-7B under two quantization strategies: “Uniform” (blue bars) and “Ours” (orange bars), across four quantization bit levels: 3, 4, 8, and 16 bits. In all three subplots, the x-axis represents “Quantization Bits” with categories ordered as 3, 4, 8, 16, while the y-axis measures “Perplexity” on a linear scale ranging from 0 to 30 in (a) and (c), and from 0 to 400 in (b). In (a) WikiText, Uniform achieves perplexities of ~30, ~27, ~27, and ~27, while Ours achieves ~22, ~19, ~18, and ~18, showing consistent improvement. In (b) PTB, Uniform scores ~410, ~320, ~300, and ~300, whereas Ours scores ~250, ~180, ~185, and ~180, again demonstrating lower perplexity across all bit levels. In (c) C4, Uniform scores ~29, ~25, ~24.5, and ~24.5, while Ours scores ~21, ~18, ~17.5, and ~17.5, maintaining a clear advantage. Across all datasets, the “Ours” method consistently yields lower perplexity than “Uniform” quantization at every bit level, with the largest relative gains observed at lower bit counts (especially 3 and 4 bits). The bars are grouped by quantization bit, with Uniform always positioned to the left of Ours within each group, and no bars are shaded or annotated beyond their color-coded legend.
model_annotations.German: The bar charts in panels (a) WikiText, (b) PTB, and (c) C4 present the perplexity of the LLaMA1-7B model evaluated on three distinct validation datasets under varying quantization bit configurations (3, 4, 8, and 16 bits), comparing two quantization strategies: “Uniform” (dark blue) and “Ours” (orange), as indicated by the legend in each panel. In all three subplots, the horizontal axis represents the number of quantization bits, arranged in ascending order from left to right, while the vertical axis denotes perplexity, with linear scales ranging from 0 to 30 in (a) and (c), and 0 to 400 in (b), with tick marks at intervals of 5 in (a) and (c), and 50 in (b). For WikiText (a), the Uniform method yields perplexity values of approximately 30, 27.5, 27, and 27 across 3, 4, 8, and 16 bits respectively, while “Ours” achieves lower values of about 22, 19, 18.5, and 18.5. In PTB (b), Uniform perplexity starts at ~410 at 3 bits, then drops to ~320, ~300, and ~300 at 4, 8, and 16 bits; “Ours” consistently performs better with values around 250, 180, 185, and 180. For C4 (c), Uniform perplexity is ~29, ~25, ~24.5, and ~24.5, whereas “Ours” reaches ~21, ~18, ~18, and ~18. In all datasets, the “Ours” method produces lower perplexity than “Uniform” across all bit widths, with the performance gap most pronounced at lower bit counts, and no bars are visually emphasized beyond color coding; the bars are grouped by quantization bit and sorted left-to-right by increasing bit count.
